title: The most famous stanza and its revisions
greek: Persian divani ('a divan, a book of poems')
short: The best-known stanza of FitzGerald's Rubaiyat; in 1859 it was XI, 'Here with a Loaf of Bread beneath the Bough, / A Flask of Wine, a Book of Verse--and Thou'.
body: In the first edition (1859) the stanza ran: 'Here with a Loaf of Bread beneath the Bough, / A Flask of Wine, a Book of Verse--and Thou / Beside me singing in the Wilderness-- / And Wilderness is Paradise enow.' From the second edition (1868) FitzGerald put the book first and changed the flask to a jug; the last line became the wishful 'Oh, Wilderness were Paradise enow!' The usual Persian source is a quatrain in the Ouseley manuscript in Oxford (Heron-Allen's no. 25), which asks for a flask of ruby wine, a divan (book of verse), half a loaf, and 'you and I seated in a ruin'. The stanza became the emblem of late-Victorian Omar-worship, quoted, parodied and printed on everything from gift-books to advertisements.

title: 'underneath the Bough'
short: The shade of a tree is FitzGerald's addition, an English pastoral setting; the Persian source places the lovers in a ruin.
body: The Persian quatrain behind the stanza has no tree; its scene is the viran, the ruin or waste place. FitzGerald's bough supplies the green shade of the English pastoral and of the earlier stanza (X in 1859) about the 'strip of Herbage strown / That just divides the desert from the sown'. A variant reading recorded by later editors (Forughi) does put the lovers in 'a corner of a garden', which is closer to FitzGerald's bough, though he could not have known it. The bough may also recall the shade-tree of the Song of Songs (2:3, 'I sat down under his shadow with great delight').

title: 'A Jug of Wine'
greek: Persian tang-i mey ('narrow-necked flask of wine')
short: The Persian asks for a narrow-necked flask of wine; FitzGerald first wrote 'Flask', then the homelier 'Jug'.
body: The Ouseley quatrain (Heron-Allen no. 25) asks for a narrow-necked flask of wine, which Heron-Allen's translation renders as ruby wine. FitzGerald's 1859 'Flask' was nearer to it; the later 'Jug' is plainer and more English, and it joins the stanza's alliteration and assonance (Book, Bough, Jug, Loaf). Wine in Khayyam's quatrains is both a real pleasure and a provocation to orthodox piety; whether it should also be read mystically, as Sufi readers of Persian poetry often read wine, was argued over by FitzGerald and his contemporaries, and FitzGerald himself insisted on the literal reading in his preface.

title: 'a Loaf of Bread'
short: The Persian asks for only half a loaf, 'enough to keep life going'; FitzGerald's whole loaf keeps the idea of simple sufficiency.
body: The Persian line asks for a 'last breath's support' (sadd-i ramaqi), half a loaf: the minimum to stay alive. A related quatrain (Sa'idi's text) offers wheaten bread and a leg of mutton. FitzGerald's 'a Loaf of Bread' turns ascetic minimum into modest picnic. The list form, book, jug, loaf and 'Thou', is the rhetorical heart of the stanza: a catalogue of few things set against the 'sultan's realm' with which the Persian quatrain compares them, a comparison FitzGerald drops in favour of Paradise.

title: 'and Thou'
greek: Persian man u tu ('I and you')
short: The addressee is unnamed and ungendered, as in Persian: a beloved, a companion, perhaps the saqi who pours the wine.
body: The Persian says simply 'I and you' (man u tu); Persian has no grammatical gender, so the companion may be male or female. FitzGerald's archaic 'Thou', separated by a dash, makes the beloved the climax of the list and the subject of the next line, 'Beside me singing'. Victorian readers usually pictured a woman; the poem's homoerotic possibilities, which scholars have discussed in relation to FitzGerald's own attachments, are left open. The dash and enjambment make 'Thou' hang at the line end before the singing begins.

title: The Wilderness
short: FitzGerald's 'Wilderness' renders the Persian viran, a ruin or desolate place; the word also carries biblical echoes for English readers.
body: Viran means something ruined or laid waste, the deserted place where outcasts and drinkers gather, far from mosque and court. FitzGerald's 'Wilderness' gives it the resonance of the English Bible, where the wilderness is the place of exile and testing, and where Isaiah promises that 'the wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad' and 'blossom as the rose' (Isaiah 35:1). The repetition across the line break ('Wilderness-- / Oh, Wilderness') is FitzGerald's, and it makes the stanza turn on a single word: the waste becomes Paradise by the presence of the beloved.

title: Paradise
greek: Avestan pairi-daeza ('walled enclosure'), via Greek paradeisos
short: 'Paradise' comes ultimately from an Old Iranian word for a walled garden, so FitzGerald's wilderness becomes a garden by etymology too.
body: English 'paradise' comes through Latin and Greek paradeisos from an Old Iranian word for an enclosure or park (Avestan pairi-daeza; OED, paradise n.). The Greek word was used for Persian royal parks and then, in the Septuagint, for the garden of Eden. FitzGerald's line thus returns the word to Persia. In the Persian quatrain the comparison is with a sultan's kingdom; FitzGerald's choice of Paradise sets earthly pleasure against the promised Paradise of religion, a contrast the sequence develops in later stanzas on 'threats of Hell and Hopes of Paradise'.

title: 'enow'
short: An archaic form of 'enough', chosen for the rhyme with Bough and Thou and for its old-fashioned ring.
body: 'Enow' is an old variant of 'enough' (OED, enow adj. and adv.), descended from Old English genoh; by FitzGerald's time it was poetic or dialectal, and it had been used chiefly with plural nouns. It allows the rhyme Bough / Thou / enow, the AABA pattern of the ruba'i. The shift from the first edition's statement 'And Wilderness is Paradise enow' to the later exclamation 'Oh, Wilderness were Paradise enow!' changes fact into wish: the subjunctive 'were' admits that the moment is imagined, not possessed, which fits the sequence's melancholy.
